bibliography.note: den Heyer C. & Kalff J. 1998. Limnol. Oceanogr. 43(4): 695–705, as cited.

claims.claim: littoral sediments mineralize about three times as fast as profundal ones
claims.location: p. 695 (PDF p. 1), Abstract; p. 698 (PDF p. 4), Table 2 and Results
claims.quote: on average, threefold higher than in the profundal sediments
claims.conditions: organic-matter (carbon) mineralization measured as DIC + CH4 accumulating over intact cores incubated in the dark at ±2 °C of in situ temperature; nine southern Quebec lakes (Eastern Townships and Laurentians), June–October 1993; Table 2 means (June–August): profundal 7 mmol C m⁻² d⁻¹ (n = 63, mean site depth 11.5 m, water 11 °C), littoral weed bed 29 (n = 67, 1.8 m, 20 °C), littoral sand 21 (n = 52, 1.9 m, 22 °C)
claims.note: The ratio is of carbon released (DIC + CH4), not oxygen consumed, and it includes the temperature difference: littoral cores sat at ~20–22 °C against ~11 °C for profundal ones; site depth, 'a surrogate variable that incorporates the effect of temperature', explained 60 % of the variation. The paper's paragraph is about the sediment oxygen sink, so it should say 'carbon mineralization' (or 'respiration'). The paper can drop 'abstract' — the full text is read.

notes: Other values: individual cores ranged −50 to 112 mmol C m⁻² d⁻¹; more than half (54–100 %) of the sediments' DIC + CH4 came from the littoral zone, yet littoral sediments were < 20 % of epilimnetic water-column-plus-sediment metabolism; in shallow and oligotrophic lakes the sediments carry a larger share of total respiration. CH4 production averaged ~3 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹ against ~14 for DIC.
